items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-10-26
items.q: You mean Alan Lomax. Alan Lomax invented him.

ctx.x: A Jelly Roll Martin. Oh, yeah. It's on the record, where he says, you can hear him say, I like whiskey. Give me some more whiskey. This fellow invented him. This man never was recognized in his life. You mean Alan Lomax. Alan Lomax invented him.
Did you ever see Jelly Roll Martin?

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-26
items.q: Alan Lomax discovered a man, well, called Jelero Martin.

ctx.x: Wait a minute, I can't hear. No, one Dirt. Tiger Rag. We did go over Tiger Rag a little bit, but...

Well, there we go again. As much has been said about the Tiger Rag, Alan Lomax discovered a man, well, called Jelero Martin. A man who's never been honored or given credit for anything. That he's done anything. Maybe he played good jazz, I don't know. But it would have to be after the original Dixieland jazz band, because I never heard him, and I never heard him today. They discovered this man, and he goes in the archers of the United States government somewhere, where they keep this folk music. Set him up two…

and then different ideas come to you, you try to put them together. My inability to learn new music put me on my own, that I had to make up my own music if I wanted to be different and have them play different tunes or play the same tune all night. Well, now I'm going to take this Tiger Rag apart. The beginning of this Tiger Rag begins with an ending that I always made to my numbers. And this is it. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da-da. Now, if anyone has any musical ears at all, they'll hear that in many other endings…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: So that the opening words of the late Jelly Roll Morton on his talk for the Library of Congress in Washington, with Alan Lomax, is wrong completely.

ctx.x: Now, they say that this, but Freddie Kepit, they make a great big story about it, that he was asked by the Victor Company to record. He says he didn't want to record because he didn't want the world to know his stuff. But they didn't know that I knew all this stuff. They thought that I was just a dumb man, that I didn't know what was going on. They imported them all. The Kepits, the Olivers, and all of them, they all died in the gutter. None of them made good. None of them could make a record. They had to steal…

So that the opening words of the late Jelly Roll Morton on his talk for the Library of Congress in Washington, with Alan Lomax, is wrong completely. He says from the very first, the first words he says on those records is, jazz started in New Orleans. And he goes on to tell about how he wrote Tiger Rag, how he named it, and how it was based on the old French quadrilles and all the rest of that stuff. Well, you've told me already, and I believe you absolutely, that that is just so much hooey.
Well, as far as him, he stole his music from the original Dixieland jazz band. You don't have to go any further than that Mellenberg Jaws.
